title: Answer to Question: On the Elections in Iran and the Reality of the Events That Followed Them
text:
Answer to Question: On the elections in Iran and the reality of the events that followed them

Question:

On 12/6/2009 elections for the presidency of the republic took place in Iran, and the current President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad won with 62.6% and his rival Mir Hossein Mousavi with 33.7%, as was officially announced in Iran. The two other rivals won small percentages. Mousavi and his supporters cast doubt on the results of the elections. On 15/6/2009 Mousavi's supporters organised protest marches and demonstrations without a permit. When the Iranian security forces dispersed the demonstrators, riots and violence broke out that led to the killing of 7 people and the wounding of 29 people, as was announced in Tehran...

So do these events indicate that an international struggle is taking place in Iran, or is it an internal struggle between centres of power over positions? And what is the extent of the presence of America and Europe in these events?

Answer:

1- The events taking place in Iran following the announcement of the election results are remarkable events. The reality of the political system in Iran, the nature of the existing institutions of the system, the wide powers of the Supreme Leader and the limited powers of the President of the Republic, all of that makes the occurrence of such escalating events a matter that deserves to be paused at.

2- Statements have appeared from the institutions of the system which indicate that the system has realised the heat of the events and that they are not ordinary, so much so that the Guardian Council of the Constitution showed something of a concession to satisfy the protesters. On 16/6/2009 the Guardian Council of the Constitution looked into the appeals relating to the elections submitted by Ahmadinejad's rivals, and their request to annul the elections and hold new elections. The spokesman of this council, Abbas-Ali Kadkhodaei, stated that it is not possible to annul the elections and hold new elections according to the law, but if the matter requires it, some of the disputed ballot papers will be recounted (Al Jazeera, 16/6/2009). The system's realisation of this heat also pushed Ahmadinejad's supporters on 16/6/2009 to undertake huge marches and demonstrations in support of their President Ahmadinejad and in condemnation of the riots and violence that had occurred the day before at the hands of the participants in Mousavi's protests.

3- The announcement by the rivals who lost in the elections, at their head Mousavi, that "severe violations" occurred in the elections, that fraud occurred, and that he does not recognise the election results, inflamed the movements in the street. Protest marches were organised, and riots and violence occurred during them at the hands of elements described as infiltrators, who tried to take over a security centre in order to obtain weapons to use, as was announced in Iran...

4- But more important than that is the Europeans' exploitation of these events. The French President Sarkozy stated: "The scale of the fraud was proportionate to the events of violence." The British Prime Minister Brown stated: "The Iranian leadership is required to refrain from violence and to respond to the legitimate grievances in the wake of the elections" (Al Jazeera, 16/6/2009). The French Foreign Minister Bernard Kouchner said: "What is happening in Iran is a deep and very important movement, which expresses a desire to rise up against tyranny, and France cannot bury its head in the sand in the face of that" (Al-Hayat, 18/6/2009), and he avoided answering whether France would recognise Ahmadinejad's legitimacy or not, despite the question being repeated to him three times. Germany, Italy and other European states followed them in raising the question of the violence and the protests in Iran and casting doubt on the election results; likewise their audio and visual media and their newspapers, condemning the violence, casting doubt on the election results and calling for non-recognition of Ahmadinejad's legitimacy, as the British newspaper The Times demanded explicitly on 16/6/2009, describing Ahmadinejad with bad descriptions: "the clumsy rustic whose head lives in paradise and his feet in corruption". Iran protested to France and to Britain, and indeed organised protests in front of the embassies of these two countries in Tehran. The Iranian embassy in Paris also protested, in a statement of its own, against "the statements which it described as hasty and irresponsible, and which indicate the interference of French officials in Iranian affairs" (the American Radio Sawa, 16/6/2009).

5- All of that indicates that the Europeans found an opportunity to exploit the protests by Mousavi and his group against the election results, and moved their agents to stir up some young men and students to infiltrate among the demonstrators and carry out riots, violence and shooting, so as to force the Iranian security forces to clash with them, in order to stir up unrest in an attempt to work against the regime. The Europeans are trying to magnify the matter as if a revolution has taken place. Demonstrations and marches began to come out without Mousavi's approval of them, and despite his call not to hold them and to cancel the marches and demonstrations that were to take place on 16/6/2009. The "Al Jazeera" correspondent Muhammad al-Bahrani mentioned on 17/6/2009 that matters had slipped out of Mousavi's hand and that Mousavi has no particular party organisation. All of that indicates that there are other forces carrying out these acts. And Iranian sources mentioned, as reported on "the Iranian Al-Alam page on 16/6/2009", that there were infiltrators among the demonstrators who carried out the acts of violence.

6- As for the American reactions to the elections, they were positive. The American President Obama said: "It is up to the Iranians to decide who will lead Iran, and we respect Iran's sovereignty, and we avoid the United States being the problem inside Iran, where the United States can sometimes be a political football" (US government page, 16/6/2009). The US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said: "The United States has refrained from commenting on Iran's elections, and we hope that they reflect the will of the Iranian people" (the American CNN, 14/6/2009). And Robert Gibbs, the White House spokesman, said: "The White House is impressed by the vigorous debates and the spirit of enthusiasm that these elections generated, especially among Iranian youth" (the American CNN, 14/6/2009). The Washington Post had announced that it had conducted a poll by two American experts indicating that Ahmadinejad would beat his rival Hossein Mousavi by a ratio of two to one (the Iranian Al-Alam page, 16/6/2009). And the Washington Post newspaper said on 16/6/2009 "that there is no conclusive evidence of fraud having occurred, which may not allow Washington or the Western capitals to challenge the result of the elections." And Ki-moon, the UN Secretary-General, stated: "There must be full respect for the will of the Iranian people" (Al Jazeera, 16/6/2009). It is understood from the statements and actions of the American officials, their media and their press, and with them the UN Secretary-General, that America is satisfied with the election of Ahmadinejad for a second term. Obama even mentioned that "there are few differences in policy between Ahmadinejad and his rival Mir Hossein Mousavi" (Reuters, 16/6/2009).

7- It is worth mentioning that Iran, in the era of Ahmadinejad's first term throughout the past four years, was in understanding with America on two important, prominent subjects, namely Afghanistan and Iraq; indeed it was going along with it, by the admission of its officials, at their head Ahmadinejad. He stated, while on his visit to New York to attend the UN meetings last year, in an interview with the New York Times newspaper on 26/9/2009: "Iran extended a helping hand to the United States with regard to Afghanistan... and our country also provided assistance to America in restoring calm and stability to Iraq." The Iranian President Ahmadinejad had visited these two countries, Afghanistan and Iraq, last year while they were under the bayonets of America and its unjust, destructive occupation of these two countries and their people. This indicates the satisfaction of Iran and its President with America's occupation of the two countries, his practical recognition of that, and his recognition of its agents whom America installed in the two countries. Indeed Iran announces with all frankness that it gives support to Karzai and to al-Maliki, that is, to America's agents whom it installed. And Ahmadinejad's presence currently serves America more than those called reformists, such as Khatami and Mousavi, because he and his current, called the conservative current, focus on the question of Shi'ism, or so the atmosphere around them suggests, which raises fears among the states of the region, especially the states whose rulers are tied to the English, in the Gulf and outside the Gulf. Morocco even cut its diplomatic relations with Iran several months ago, on the charge that Iran supports Shi'ism and stirs up unrest in it. And the ruler of Jordan, Abdullah II, had spoken about the Iranian threat under what he called the Shia crescent. All of that serves America, so that it can control these countries by frightening them with Iran's Shi'ism as a pretext for America remaining in the region to protect these states from Iran! At the same time America fans division among the Muslims by playing on the string of Iran's alleged spreading of Shi'ism, and consequently by stirring up madhhab-based and sectarian fanaticisms.

8- As for the American reactions to what followed the election process of demonstrations and marches in which violence occurred, Obama stated: "I said earlier that I have deep concern about the subject of the elections." And he added: "Given the history of American-Iranian relations, it would not be productive for the American President to interfere in the Iranian elections." And that he hopes "that the Iranian people will take peaceful steps so that they are able to express their aspirations" (AFP, 16/6/2009). Even his deputy Joseph Biden, although he said that this result raises many questions, added: "The United States does not have sufficient evidence to give a final judgement," and he said that the United States is ready for dialogue with Iran (BBC, 16/6/2009). These statements reveal a non-accusatory tone and a soft tone towards Iran. Some have criticised the position of the American media, especially the major ones such as CNN, Fox News and others, for their silence towards what is happening in Iran, while they are famous for covering events and magnifying them, if that is required, in what serves American policy. Meanwhile the Western European media, at their head the British Broadcasting Corporation, visual, audio and electronic, are leading a huge campaign magnifying the events in Iran. And "the Iranian Foreign Ministry accused Western media, accusing them of being spokesmen for those carrying out the riots" (Asharq Al-Awsat, 18/6/2009).

9- What has preceded indicates that the fingerprints of the international struggle between America and Europe are apparent in Iran. The states of Europe, at their head France and Britain, are working as much as they can to stir up the protests in this period, by planting their agents and stirring up the people through all their political and media means, in an attempt to destabilise the situation in Iran, and in a weak attempt to bring down the regime there and bring in their agents. It is not expected that they will succeed in this currently, because the situation is still firmly in the hands of those who go in the American orbit, whether they are reformists or conservatives. Moreover, there are no apparent forces of the Europeans working in the Iranian arena; rather their agents are hiding, waiting for opportunities, as appeared in these events.

This is clear from the European and American reactions. Europe is at the peak of its agitation over what is happening, and tension is clear in its actions and statements, whereas America is calm towards what is happening. Whereas if matters in Iran were going contrary to what America wants, or the regime in Iran were going against the American current, or America had an interest in change in Iran, it would have raised the world against the Iranian regime and its leadership, and particularly Ahmadinejad, and would not have let it settle; it would have ridden the wave of incitement as the states of Europe are doing, would have magnified matters and fabricated lies, and its media would not have been silent for a single moment, and it is famous for that, as they did against Saddam until they occupied Iraq and destroyed it, and as they did against the Taliban until they occupied Afghanistan and destroyed it too, and killed millions of the people of these two Muslim countries.

10- Although the fingerprints of the international struggle are clear, the struggle of the internal centres of power is likewise visible to the eye. What is understood from what followed the announcement of the election results, from Mousavi's current and those behind him, such as Rafsanjani, Khatami and Nateq-Nouri, is that they could not digest their defeat, just as Rafsanjani himself was defeated in the previous elections before Ahmadinejad. So they wanted to create confusion so that the elections would be repeated. The struggle between the so-called reformist current, at its head Rafsanjani and Khatami and their representative in these elections Mousavi, and the current of the so-called conservatives, at its head Ahmadinejad, supported by the Supreme Leader of the Iranian Republic Ali Khamenei and others of the Shia scholars, is an internal struggle over leadership and interests and over bringing about some internal changes, or what are called reforms. The struggle between them is raging to its utmost limits, as it appears. Indeed "Ahmadinejad likened Rafsanjani and the former Interior Minister Nateq-Nouri to the role of Talha and al-Zubayr in the Battle of the Camel against Imam Ali, and demanded that they be uprooted from the political arena" (the London Al-Hayat, 18/6/2009). But they, that is the two currents, are agreed in foreign policy, except in some styles such as the use of rhetoric.

For this reason Obama said that there is no great difference between Ahmadinejad and Mousavi, but rather the difference between them is small. And since the Supreme Leader of the Republic, Ali Khamenei, in a statement he issued on 16/6/2009, showed that he supports Ahmadinejad, blessed his election, congratulated him on his success, called on the people to rally around him, and mentioned that he will achieve progress and advancement for the country and guarantee national security, activity and vitality, then continued his words in his statement by saying: "And there is no doubt that this too is a divine choice, success in which will bring the mercy of Allah the Exalted" (the Iranian Al-Alam page, 18/6/2009); and likewise the Speaker of the Shura Council, Ali Larijani, and the head of the judiciary, Hashemi Shahroudi, supported and blessed him; all of that will consolidate Ahmadinejad's authority and establish the legitimacy of his election. It is most likely that some ballot boxes will be re-examined as a solution to the objections and protests, but that will not change the result. Even so, the internal struggle of the centres of power has found a path for itself that is not easy to close, even if it falls silent...
